newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: IMF in final round of loan talks with Pakistan.
newsitem.headline: IMF in final round of loan talks with Pakistan.

text.p: An International Monetary Fund director for the Middle East arrived in Islamabad on Monday to conclude discussions with Pakistani officials for a new medium-term loan, a government official said.

The Finance Ministry official said Paul Chabrier arrived to lead an IMF team into the final round of policy-level discussions with Pakistan for a $1.2 billion to $1.5 billion, three-year enhanced structural adjustment facility (ESAF) loan.
An IMF team started technical discussions with Pakistani officials on July 10 on various aspects of Pakistan's economy and budget for fiscal 1997/98 (July-June) announced in June.
The talks will continue until Wednesday after which Charbier and his team will prepare the draft of a policy framework paper for consideration of the IMF executive board.

Finance Minister Sartaj Aziz has said the talks will result in a new loan for Pakistan because Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's government has already undertaken strucutural reforms ahead of IMF's initial expectations.
Local newspapers have quoted Pakistani officials as saying that Islamabad will be able to secure the loan because its economic indicators, targets and performence are in line with the IMF.
They say revenue and spending targets laid out in the 1997/98 budget are generally consistent with the reform programme, but some fine-tuning may be needed.

Pakistan signed a $1.5 billion, three-year ESAF lending programme with the IMF in February 1994, but the Fund halted disbursements after the former government led by then prime minister Benazir Bhutto announced a 1995/96 budget that failed to meet agreed targets.
A balance of payments crisis in October 1995 forced the Bhutto government to seek an IMF standby loan, which was suspended in March last year, again because of missed targets.

The standby was resumed and expanded in December after a caretaker government took over from the dismissed Bhutto, but the IMF halted it in March when Sharif's government said the targets were out of reach.
At that time the IMF welcomed Sharif's plans for structural reform, including tax and tax administration reform, faster privatisation, and revival of industry and farming.
